cards.h: The base of every environment question
cards.b:
Ecology appears in UPSC Prelims almost every year. Questions on food chains, pyramids, keystone species and biomagnification are routine.

GS Paper III also uses these ideas. Pollution, climate and biodiversity answers all rest on how an ecosystem works. If energy flow is clear, much of the syllabus becomes easy.

Ecology is the study of how organisms relate to each other and to their surroundings. The word was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866. The term ecosystem was coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935.

The levels run from organism to population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. An ecosystem has abiotic parts (light, soil, water) and biotic parts: producers, consumers and decomposers.

A grazing food chain starts with green plants and moves to herbivores and carnivores. A detritus food chain starts with dead matter, eaten by earthworms and fungi. On land, much more energy flows through the detritus chain.

Each feeding level is a trophic level. Real ecosystems form a food web with many linked chains. A web is more stable because an animal can switch food if one source fails.

Sunlight is the only input. Producers capture only a small part of it. Raymond Lindeman (1942) showed that about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat in respiration.

So energy flow is one-way. Nutrients cycle, but energy does not. This is also why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.

cards.h: GPP, NPP and who is most productive
cards.b:
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total energy fixed by producers. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the energy used by plants in respiration. NPP is the food available to consumers.

Per unit area, estuaries, coral reefs and tropical rainforests are among the most productive. Open oceans are poor per area but huge in total because they cover so much of Earth.

The pyramid of energy is always upright. Energy cannot increase going up.

The pyramid of biomass is inverted in the sea. Tiny phytoplankton have a small standing crop but multiply fast, and they feed a larger mass of zooplankton and fish. The pyramid of numbers can be inverted too: one big tree supports thousands of insects.

Some substances are not broken down or excreted: DDT, mercury, cadmium. They build up in fat or tissue. This is bioaccumulation. When the concentration rises at each higher trophic level, it is biomagnification.

Top predators suffer most. DDT thinned the eggshells of eagles and falcons. Mercury caused Minamata disease in Japan (1956). Cadmium caused Itai-itai disease.

Habitat is where an organism lives. Niche is its role: what it eats, where it lives and how it behaves. A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers. Robert Paine (1966) showed this with the starfish Pisaster on rocky shores.

An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems, such as mangroves between land and sea. It often holds more species. This is the edge effect.

India’s vultures crashed by over 95 percent in the 1990s. The cause was diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle. Vultures ate the carcasses and died of kidney failure.

Without vultures, carcasses rotted, stray dogs increased and rabies risk rose. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. This is a clean example of how one lost scavenger breaks the detritus link.

The Sundarbans, Western Ghats and Chilika are all good examples of linked food webs under stress.

Mains-style: “Ecosystem services are the lifeline of human welfare. Discuss with Indian examples.” Structure: define services (provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting); give Indian cases (mangroves as storm buffers, wetlands as flood sponges, pollinators); name the threat; end with policy (PES, Green Credit).

Mains-style: “Why is biomagnification a concern for human health?” Define, give DDT and mercury, link to Indian pesticide use, suggest bans and organic methods.

Prelims tip: Energy pyramids are always upright. Biomass pyramids can be inverted only in aquatic systems. Learn who coined each term.

quiz.w: Tansley coined it in 1935. Haeckel coined ecology; Lindeman gave the ten percent law.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of energy passes to the next trophic level?
quiz.w: The ten percent law. Most energy is lost as heat in respiration.

o: Pyramid of biomass in the sea
Pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem
Pyramid of numbers in a pond
quiz.w: Energy cannot increase going up a chain, so its pyramid is always upright.
Net primary productivity is gross productivity minus what plants burn in respiration.

quiz.q: In terrestrial ecosystems, most energy flows through the:
quiz.w: Much plant matter is not grazed and is eaten by decomposers after death.

quiz.q: The starfish Pisaster was used by Paine to show the idea of:
quiz.w: Removing the starfish caused mussels to take over and reduced diversity.

quiz.q: Itai-itai disease is linked to which metal?
quiz.w: Cadmium caused Itai-itai in Japan. Mercury caused Minamata.

quiz.q: The transition zone between two ecosystems is called:
quiz.w: An ecotone sits between ecosystems and often shows the edge effect.

quiz.q: The drug that nearly wiped out India’s vultures was:
quiz.w: Diclofenac in cattle carcasses caused kidney failure in vultures. It was banned for veterinary use in 2006.

o: Increase in energy at higher levels
Growth of algae in a lake
Concentration of a persistent substance rises at higher trophic levels
quiz.w: Persistent toxins accumulate more at each higher level, so top predators carry the most.
